correctness.rationale: The polar is an explicit central section of the cube. Its vertex parity class yields a nonoverlapping conical triangulation: respectively n*C(n-1,floor((n-1)/2)) equal-volume simplices. Gram determinant 1/n and exact simplex Dirichlet second moments give both volume and scalar covariance. Substitution against the regular cross-polytope gives two Wallis-factor ratios. The Wallis product with elementary exponential bounds settles all infinite dimensions; exact rational comparisons settle the finitely many remaining cases. Independent low-dimensional Qhull integrations confirm volume and radial moments for n=3..8; neither those tests nor numerical limit evaluations are used to infer the infinite result.

originality.rationale: The assessed theorem is not the known volume or construction. It gives the exact uniform-volume covariance of the canonical symmetric projected simplex, an all-dimensional strict comparison with the same-dimensional regular cross-polytope, the exceptional dimensions n=4 and 6, and a nonzero first-order deficit. Full text of the source construction, the directly relevant arbitrary-projection theorem, and modern isotropic-extremality work was materially compared; searches included aliases and stronger general statements. The result has residual risk of equivalent earlier computations under projection terminology; novelty is a best-knowledge judgment, not an independence claim.
residual_risks: Older probability or convex-geometric computations might encode these second moments under the labels zero-sum quotient of \(\ell_1^n\), projection body, or symmetrized simplex.
The full literature is not exhaustively indexed; no independent external referee has checked the proof.

value.rationale: The isotropic constant is a natural affine-invariant spreading statistic of a polytope, and the maximal-volume Bier body is canonically a highly symmetric hyperplane projection of a cross-polytope. The comparison has a sharp and unexpected low-dimensional reversal at precisely n=4 and n=6, while a nonzero negative first-order asymptotic constant quantifies convergence to the same cross-polytope limit. This distinguishes finite-dimensional behavior of canonical projections rather than recomputing only volume or a known radius.
